genres.name: Lonnie Donegan: Rock Island Line
genres.text: Lonnie Donegan, banjo player in Chris Barber's jazz band, recorded an old American work song with guitar, washboard and bass. In early January 1956 Rock Island Line entered the British chart, and it became a hit in America too. Thousands of British teenagers concluded that you could start a band with three chords and household objects. That is how the skiffle craze began, and John Lennon's group grew out of it.
genres.listen: Listen to how Donegan keeps pushing the tempo up, like a train gathering speed. You need little more than a few chords and a driving rhythm.

genres.name: Elvis Presley: Heartbreak Hotel
genres.text: Heartbreak Hotel was Presley's first single for RCA and his first big national hit. In Liverpool the fifteen-year-old John Lennon heard the song, and according to him nothing before it had really got through to him. The recording sounds hollow and ghostly because of the echo from a hallway next to the studio in Nashville. For Lennon, McCartney and Harrison, Elvis became the model of what a rock singer could be.
genres.listen: Listen to the empty space around the voice: lots of echo, a sparse bass and a piano that only comes in late.

genres.name: Little Richard: Long Tall Sally
genres.text: Little Richard recorded Long Tall Sally in Cosimo Matassa's J&M studio in New Orleans, with hammering piano and saxophones. The song came out in March 1956 and spent weeks at the top of the American rhythm-and-blues chart. Paul McCartney learned his screaming falsetto cry, and the Beatles played the song for years. It was the last song of their very last paid concert, at Candlestick Park in 1966.
genres.listen: Hear how Little Richard screams over a band playing at full speed. Compare his shrieks with McCartney's in the Beatles version from Candlestick Park.

genres.name: Chuck Berry: Roll Over Beethoven
genres.text: Chuck Berry wrote his own lyrics about teenagers, cars and radio, and played guitar riffs that everyone wanted to copy. Roll Over Beethoven came out in May 1956 on Chess in Chicago and cheerfully says goodbye to classical music. For the Beatles, Berry was proof that a rock 'n' roll artist could write his own songs. George Harrison sang Roll Over Beethoven on With the Beatles.
genres.listen: Listen to the guitar intro: a few fast double stops that set the tempo at once. Harrison later played that intro back almost note for note.

genres.name: Stockhausen: Gesang der Jünglinge
genres.text: In the electronic studio of the WDR in Cologne, Karlheinz Stockhausen mixed the recorded voice of a boy with electronic sounds. Gesang der Jünglinge premiered on 30 May 1956. Ten years later Paul McCartney played such records to the other Beatles, and Stockhausen got a place on the cover of Sgt. Pepper. His idea that you can cut up and distort sound on tape echoes in Tomorrow Never Knows and Revolution 9.
genres.listen: Try to follow when you hear a real boy's voice and when an electronic sound. Where is the border?

genres.name: The Quarrymen
genres.text: During the skiffle craze the sixteen-year-old John Lennon started a band with school friends. They named themselves after his school, Quarry Bank High School. Lennon played guitar with banjo chords that his mother Julia had taught him, others played a washboard and a tea-chest bass. The line-up changed constantly. Sources differ on the exact starting date, but it began in late 1956, when skiffle was at its peak all over Great Britain.

genres.name: The Everly Brothers: Bye Bye Love
genres.text: Don and Phil Everly sang in tight two-part harmony, a style from their parents' country music. Bye Bye Love came out in the spring of 1957 on Cadence and became a big hit in America and England. Lennon and McCartney practised their harmony singing on Everly records. Those two voices moving right next to each other can be heard in early Beatles songs such as Please Please Me and This Boy.
genres.listen: Follow the two voices in the chorus: they sing the same words at different pitches, always close together.

tracks.title: All I Have to Do Is Dream

genres.name: Buddy Holly & The Crickets
genres.text: Buddy Holly wrote his own songs, wore glasses and played with a fixed group: two guitars, bass and drums. Lennon found that reassuring: you did not have to look like Elvis. That'll Be the Day, recorded in Norman Petty's studio in Clovis, came out on 27 May 1957. The Quarrymen recorded it a year later, and the name The Beatles is a nod to Holly's band The Crickets.
genres.listen: Compare That'll Be the Day by The Crickets with the Quarrymen's version from 1958. How close do the Liverpool teenagers get to their example?

genres.name: Lennon meets McCartney
genres.text: On Saturday 6 July 1957 the Quarrymen played at the summer fête of St Peter's Church in Woolton. Between the sets a friend introduced the fifteen-year-old Paul McCartney to Lennon. McCartney played Twenty Flight Rock by Eddie Cochran and knew all the words. Lennon had to choose: a better musician in the band, or stay the boss himself. He chose the band. A local boy recorded part of the performance that day.
genres.listen: Lennon sang Come Go with Me by The Del-Vikings on stage that afternoon, with words he made up himself. Twenty Flight Rock is the song with which McCartney made an impression.

genres.name: George Harrison joins
genres.text: McCartney brought along his school friend George Harrison, who was only fourteen. Lennon thought he was too young, but according to the well-known story Harrison played the guitar instrumental Raunchy flawlessly on the top deck of a bus. After that he was allowed to stay. The usual date is 6 February 1958, but some researchers think it was as early as December 1957. With Harrison the band had a real lead guitarist.
genres.listen: Raunchy by Bill Justis is the piece with which Harrison auditioned: a simple, twangy guitar melody with saxophone.

genres.name: The Quarrymen's acetate record
genres.text: For a few shillings the group cut one acetate disc at Percy Phillips's studio in Kensington, Liverpool. Lennon, McCartney, Harrison, pianist John Lowe and drummer Colin Hanton played That'll Be the Day and In Spite of All the Danger, a song by McCartney and Harrison. The date is probably 12 July 1958. Pianist John Lowe kept the disc for over twenty years, until McCartney bought it in 1981. It appeared in 1995 on Anthology 1.
genres.listen: In Spite of All the Danger is a slow ballad in 12/8, with Harrison on guitar. You hear teenagers imitating Elvis and Buddy Holly as well as they can.

tracks.title: In Spite of All the Danger

genres.name: Johnny and the Moondogs
genres.text: In late 1958 Lennon, McCartney and Harrison, as Johnny and the Moondogs, took part in TV Star Search, a talent contest run by Carroll Levis at the Hippodrome in Manchester. They played Think It Over by Buddy Holly. The winner was chosen with an applause meter, but they had to leave to catch the last train to Liverpool. Older books say 1959, but researcher Mark Lewisohn places it in 1958.
genres.listen: Listen for the little piano solo in the middle and the backing vocals. The Moondogs had to make do with guitars and their own three voices.

genres.name: The Casbah Coffee Club

place.name: Casbah Coffee Club, Hayman's Green, West Derby

genres.text: On 29 August 1959 Mona Best opened the Casbah Coffee Club in the cellar of her large house in West Derby, Liverpool, meant for her son Pete and his friends. Lennon, McCartney and Harrison had helped paint it. On opening night they played as The Quarrymen, without a drummer and with one microphone, for some three hundred young people. A year later Pete Best became their drummer.

genres.name: Tour of Scotland
genres.text: In May 1960 Lennon, McCartney, Harrison, Sutcliffe and drummer Tommy Moore were allowed to back the singer Johnny Gentle for over a week on a tour of Scotland. Pop manager Larry Parnes had chosen them after an audition. The posters said only 'Johnny Gentle and his group'. They played in small halls in places such as Alloa, Inverness and Fraserburgh. It was their first real tour, and soon afterwards Moore quit as drummer.

genres.name: Hamburg: the Indra
genres.text: On 17 August 1960 the Beatles played for the first time at the Indra, a small club on the Grosse Freiheit in Hamburg. Pete Best had been hired as drummer a few days earlier. They played 48 nights, often four and a half hours a night, and slept behind a cinema screen. Club owner Bruno Koschmider shouted 'mach Schau!'. Over five stints until late 1962 they became a hard, tight live band in Hamburg.

genres.name: Litherland Town Hall
genres.text: On 27 December 1960, just back from Hamburg, the Beatles played at Litherland Town Hall, near Liverpool. The poster said 'Direct from Hamburg', and many in the audience thought it was a German band. As soon as McCartney started Long Tall Sally, the crowd surged towards the stage. The band got six pounds, and promoter Brian Kelly booked them for more nights at once. Many experts see this as the start of their fame in Liverpool.
genres.listen: Hear the screaming voice of Little Richard. This was the kind of fast rock 'n' roll the Beatles had played night after night in Hamburg.

genres.name: The Cavern Club
genres.text: The Cavern was a damp cellar in Mathew Street, which began as a jazz club. On 9 February 1961 the Beatles played their first lunchtime session there, for a fee of five pounds. Until August 1963 they appeared there almost 300 times. Office workers came to watch in their lunch break. Sweat ran down the walls and the amplifiers sometimes failed. This is where Brian Epstein saw the band for the first time.

genres.name: Motown and girl groups
genres.text: Berry Gordy built a record label in Detroit like a factory, with fixed songwriters and a fixed house band. Please Mr. Postman by The Marvelettes, released on 21 August 1961, became Motown's first number 1 on the American pop chart. The Beatles loved these records. With the Beatles contains three Motown covers: Please Mister Postman, You've Really Got a Hold on Me and Money.
genres.listen: Listen to the call and response between lead singer and backing chorus in Please Mr. Postman. The Beatles used the same trick in their own songs.

tracks.title: You've Really Got a Hold on Me

genres.name: My Bonnie
genres.text: In June 1961 the Beatles recorded a few songs in Hamburg with producer Bert Kaempfert, as backing band for the singer Tony Sheridan. The label said not The Beatles but The Beat Brothers, because 'Beatles' sounded too much like a vulgar word in German. My Bonnie, a Scottish folk song turned rock 'n' roll, came out in October 1961 on Polydor. Customers asked for it in Epstein's record shop.
genres.listen: The song starts as a solemn ballad and then switches to rock 'n' roll. Listen to Pete Best's drums.

genres.name: Brian Epstein at The Cavern
genres.text: Brian Epstein managed the record department of NEMS, his family's shop in Liverpool. On 9 November 1961 he went to a lunchtime session at The Cavern to see the band that customers kept asking about. He was hooked at once. In January 1962 the Beatles signed a contract with him. Epstein put them in suits, made them bow after every song and went knocking on the doors of record companies in London.

genres.name: The Decca audition
genres.text: On New Year's Day 1962 the Beatles played fifteen songs in about an hour in the Decca studio in West Hampstead, mostly covers and a few songs of their own. They were nervous after a long drive through the snow. Decca chose Brian Poole and the Tremeloes, from near London. Epstein said later that he had been told guitar groups were going out of fashion.
genres.listen: Searchin' and Like Dreamers Do come from the audition tape. They were released in 1995 on Anthology 1. Does the band already sound like a group that deserves a contract?

genres.name: The Isley Brothers: Twist and Shout
genres.text: Twist and Shout was written by Phil Medley and Bert Berns. The Isley Brothers' version came out in the spring of 1962 on the Wand label and became their first top 40 hit. The song leans on three chords that keep repeating and vocals full of gospel shouts. The Beatles made it their closer, and it became the last song of their first album.
genres.listen: Listen to the build-up just before the end: the voices pile up note by note. The Beatles took over that moment literally.

genres.name: George Martin
genres.text: George Martin ran Parlophone, EMI's small comedy and classical label. He had studied oboe and piano and had made records with Peter Sellers. On 6 June 1962 the Beatles came to the EMI studio on Abbey Road for the first time. Martin still found their songs mediocre, but their humour appealed to him. He became their producer and translated their ideas into arrangements, strings and studio tricks.
genres.listen: Besame Mucho, on Anthology 1, comes from that first session at EMI on 6 June 1962, still with Pete Best on drums.

genres.name: Ringo Starr joins
genres.text: In mid-August 1962 drummer Pete Best was fired. His replacement was Ringo Starr, who knew the band from Hamburg, where he drummed with Rory Storm and the Hurricanes. On 18 August 1962 Starr played his first official gig as a Beatle, at Hulme Hall in Port Sunlight. Best's fans were angry and there was shouting at The Cavern. With Lennon, McCartney, Harrison and Starr the permanent line-up was complete.

genres.name: Love Me Do
genres.text: Love Me Do, the first Beatles single, came out on 5 October 1962 on Parlophone. It is a simple song on two chords with a harmonica part by Lennon. Martin had doubts about Ringo and had it recorded again with session drummer Andy White. That is why two versions exist. The song reached number 17 in England, a modest start, but it brought the band onto radio and television.
genres.listen: Listen to the harmonica: Lennon played one partly because Bruce Channel's Hey! Baby had one. Do you hear a tambourine? Then it is the version with Andy White.

genres.name: Please Please Me
genres.text: Lennon wrote Please Please Me as a slow ballad in the style of Roy Orbison. George Martin found it dull and had it played much faster. After the recording he reportedly said they had just made their first number 1. The single came out on 11 January 1963 and reached the top of most British charts. The song showed what a producer can change in a song.
genres.listen: Listen to the question and answer between voice and chorus ('come on, come on') and to the high harmony that McCartney sings above Lennon.

genres.name: Abbey Road Studio Two: an album in one day
genres.text: On 11 February 1963 the band recorded ten songs for their first album in about twelve hours in EMI's Studio Two on Abbey Road. They played almost everything live, as at The Cavern, on a two-track recorder. Lennon had a cold and sucked throat lozenges. Twist and Shout came last of all, in one take, because his voice was gone afterwards. Studio Two became their regular workplace.
genres.listen: In Twist and Shout you hear Lennon's voice almost break. A second attempt was not possible.

genres.name: Please Please Me
genres.text: The first album came out on 22 March 1963. It contains the four single sides and the ten songs from the session of 11 February: eight songs of their own and six covers of American rhythm and blues and girl groups. It sounds like a club night in Liverpool. The album spent thirty weeks at number 1 on the British album chart. It was the first of eleven number 1 albums in England.
genres.listen: I Saw Her Standing There begins with McCartney counting in: 'one, two, three, four!' That is how a record that was almost recorded live opens.

genres.name: Bob Dylan: The Freewheelin'
genres.text: On The Freewheelin' Bob Dylan a young folk singer sings alone with guitar and harmonica, about war, injustice and love. The Beatles heard the record in Paris in January 1964 and played it to death. Dylan showed them that a pop song could be about something other than being in love. Lennon then wrote more personal lyrics, such as I'm a Loser and You've Got to Hide Your Love Away.
genres.listen: Listen to Blowin' in the Wind: just voice, guitar and harmonica, and a lyric that mostly asks questions.

genres.name: She Loves You
genres.text: She Loves You came out on 23 August 1963 and became the best-selling single of the sixties in England. The song starts straight away with the chorus and a drum roll from Ringo. The 'yeah, yeah, yeah' became the trademark of Beatlemania. Remarkable is the final chord with an added sixth, which George Martin thought old-fashioned, something from Glenn Miller. The band insisted, and the chord stayed.
genres.listen: Listen to the ending: the three voices finish on a chord with an extra note in it, which George Martin thought old-fashioned.

genres.name: Sunday Night at the London Palladium
genres.text: On 13 October 1963 the Beatles appeared on Sunday Night at the London Palladium, one of the most popular TV programmes in England. About fifteen million people watched. Outside the theatre screaming fans were waiting. The next day's papers wrote about the start of Beatlemania, and the word stuck. A few weeks later they played for the royal family at the Royal Variety Performance.
genres.listen: From Me to You and I'll Get You were in their Palladium set. Hear how short and compact their songs still are in 1963: around two minutes.

genres.name: Four-track recording
genres.text: Until the autumn of 1963 EMI recorded the Beatles on two tracks: band on one, vocals on the other. On 17 October 1963 they used a four-track machine for the first time, for I Want to Hold Your Hand and This Boy. Now they could record a backing track and add vocals, handclaps and extra guitars later. That was the beginning of the studio as a workshop.
genres.listen: In I Want to Hold Your Hand, listen for the handclaps and the separate vocal parts: those are later additions on the extra tracks.

tracks.title: I Want to Hold Your Hand

genres.name: Royal Variety Performance
genres.text: On 4 November 1963 the Beatles played at the Royal Variety Performance at the Prince of Wales Theatre in London, with the Queen Mother and Princess Margaret in the audience. Before the last song, Twist and Shout, Lennon asked the people in the cheap seats to clap: 'the rest of you can just rattle your jewellery'. On 10 November more than twenty million Britons watched the broadcast on ITV.
genres.listen: This is the real recording from the theatre. Hear the polite applause and how Lennon sings at the top of his voice, even for a distinguished audience.

genres.name: With the Beatles
genres.text: The second album came out on 22 November 1963, the day President Kennedy was assassinated. The cover shows four half-lit faces in black and white, photographed by Robert Freeman. There were already hundreds of thousands of advance orders. Besides their own songs it has covers of Chuck Berry and three Motown songs. Harrison made his debut as a songwriter with Don't Bother Me.
genres.listen: Compare It Won't Be Long, a song of their own with call and response, with the Motown cover Money: audibly the same school.

genres.name: I Want to Hold Your Hand
genres.text: Lennon and McCartney wrote I Want to Hold Your Hand at a piano in the basement of the Asher family, the parents of McCartney's girlfriend Jane. In England the single came out on 29 November 1963. Capitol released it in America in late December, and in early February 1964 it was number 1. That opened the door to the Ed Sullivan Show and the British Invasion.
genres.listen: Listen for the handclaps and the moment the vocals go up at 'I can't hide'. Bob Dylan heard 'I get high' there.

tracks.title: I Want to Hold Your Hand

genres.name: The Ed Sullivan Show
genres.text: Two days after arriving at JFK, the Beatles appeared on The Ed Sullivan Show on 9 February 1964. About 73 million Americans watched, a record at the time. They opened with All My Loving. During Till There Was You their names appeared on screen, with the words 'sorry girls, he's married' next to Lennon. Many who later started a band said it began that evening.
genres.listen: All My Loving and Till There Was You were the first two songs America saw. One a fast pop song, the other a musical number: Epstein wanted to show that the band could do both.

genres.name: First American concert
genres.text: On 11 February 1964 the Beatles gave their first concert in America, at the Washington Coliseum, a sports arena. They stood in the middle, as in a boxing ring, and the stage was turned between songs so that every side could see the band. Ringo had to turn his drum kit himself each time. Fans threw jelly beans, because Harrison had once said he liked them.

genres.name: Can't Buy Me Love
genres.text: McCartney wrote Can't Buy Me Love in Paris, where the band played at the Olympia for three weeks in January 1964. It was also recorded there, in an EMI studio. The single came out in March 1964, with over two million advance orders in America. In early April the Beatles occupied the top five places on the Billboard Hot 100. That had never been seen before.
genres.listen: The song starts with the chorus and is built on a twelve-bar blues. Can you hear the blues pattern?

genres.name: Blokker, 1964
genres.text: In early June 1964 the Beatles were in the Netherlands, without Ringo, who was ill. Drummer Jimmie Nicol stood in. On 5 June they recorded a TV performance in Hillegom for the VARA, and the day after they took a boat tour through the Amsterdam canals. On 6 June they played two concerts in the auction hall in Blokker, for some 2,000 and 7,000 visitors. They were their only concerts in the Netherlands.

genres.name: A Hard Day's Night (film)
genres.text: A Hard Day's Night premiered on 6 July 1964 at the London Pavilion. Director Richard Lester filmed a few frantic days in the life of the band in black and white and in a documentary-like style. The title comes from a phrase Ringo said after a long working day. The film, with its fast cutting to music, is often called a forerunner of the music video.
genres.listen: In the film the band plays I Should Have Known Better in a train carriage. Listen for the harmonica and the twelve-string guitar.

genres.name: A Hard Day's Night
genres.text: A Hard Day's Night, released on 10 July 1964, was the first album with only their own songs, all by Lennon and McCartney. Harrison plays a twelve-string Rickenbacker, which defines the sound of the record. The opening chord of the title song has become famous: anyone who wants to copy it exactly has to know who plays which note, and they still do not agree on that.
genres.listen: Play the first chord of A Hard Day's Night a few times. Which notes do you hear? Then listen to the acoustic guitars in And I Love Her.

genres.name: The first American tour
genres.text: On 19 August 1964 the first real tour of North America began at the Cow Palace in San Francisco: over thirty concerts in a month. They played short sets, about half an hour, through small amplifiers and the venue's public address system. Capitol recorded the concert at the Hollywood Bowl on 23 August, but the screaming was so loud that the recording was not released until 1977.
genres.listen: Twist and Shout comes from Live at the Hollywood Bowl, with recordings from 1964 and 1965. Hear what the band was playing against: the audience sounds almost as loud as the music.

genres.name: Bob Dylan at the Delmonico
genres.text: During the American tour Bob Dylan came to the Delmonico Hotel in New York on 28 August 1964. He thought the Beatles already smoked cannabis, because he heard 'I get high' in I Want to Hold Your Hand instead of 'I can't hide'. That evening they smoked together. The meeting was the start of mutual influence: the Beatles wrote more personally, and Dylan went electric a year later.
genres.listen: You've Got to Hide Your Love Away is Lennon's Dylan song: acoustic guitar, a flute and a singing style that winks at Dylan.

tracks.title: You've Got to Hide Your Love Away

genres.name: Feedback in I Feel Fine
genres.text: On 18 October 1964 the band recorded I Feel Fine. The song begins with a humming tone: feedback, a sound that arises when a guitar is too close to an amplifier and amplifies itself. Lennon later said proudly that it was the first time feedback was put on a record on purpose. A few years later it was a fixed part of rock.
genres.listen: Hear the first seconds of I Feel Fine: one bass note from McCartney, followed by the hum of Lennon's guitar, and only then the riff.

genres.name: Beatles for Sale
genres.text: Beatles for Sale was made in between tours and came out on 4 December 1964. On the cover four tired young men look out in autumn. It has six covers, because there was no time for more songs of their own. Even so, Dylan's influence is audible in Lennon's gloomy lyrics, such as I'm a Loser. Eight Days a Week is one of the first pop songs to begin with a fade-in.
genres.listen: Listen to the start of Eight Days a Week: the song slowly emerges from silence. In I'm a Loser you hear Lennon as Dylan.

genres.name: Ticket to Ride
genres.text: Ticket to Ride came out on 9 April 1965. It sounds heavier and slower than the early hits, with a ringing twelve-string guitar, a drum part that keeps stumbling and a long drawn-out ending. Lennon later called it one of the first heavy metal records, half joking. The song is also in the film Help!, in a scene in the snow of Austria.
genres.listen: Listen to Ringo's drum pattern: it falters and catches again and again, as if the song does not want to simply keep going.

genres.name: Help! (film)
genres.text: Help!, again directed by Richard Lester, was in colour and had a bigger budget. In the film a sect chases the band for a sacrificial ring that is stuck on Ringo's finger. Filming took place in the Bahamas and in the snow of Obertauern in Austria. The premiere was on 29 July 1965 in London. The band said later that they were often stoned during filming.
genres.listen: Another Girl plays in the film on the beach in the Bahamas. Listen to the short guitar runs by McCartney himself.

tracks.title: You're Going to Lose That Girl

genres.name: Help!
genres.text: The fifth album came out on 6 August 1965. The first side is the soundtrack of the film Help!, the second contains other songs, including Yesterday. Lennon said later that the title song was a real cry for help, hidden in a cheerful tempo. Country and folk can also be heard, as in I've Just Seen a Face. The album became their fifth number 1 in England.
genres.listen: Listen to the words of Help! and notice the contrast with the upbeat tempo. Lennon later wanted to redo it more slowly.

genres.name: Shea Stadium
genres.text: On 15 August 1965 the Beatles played at the baseball stadium Shea Stadium in New York for over 55,000 people, at the time a record for a pop concert. The band stood on a stage in the middle of the field and played through the stadium's loudspeakers. Because of the screaming they hardly heard themselves. The concert showed how big pop had become, and also that the technology was not yet ready for stadium concerts.

genres.name: Yesterday
genres.text: McCartney woke up with the melody in his head and at first thought he had heard it somewhere. For a while he sang 'scrambled eggs' to it. On 14 June 1965 he recorded Yesterday alone with an acoustic guitar, and three days later Martin added a string quartet. In England it was on Help!, in America it became a number 1 single in September 1965. It became one of the most covered songs ever.
genres.listen: No drums, no other Beatles: just McCartney, a guitar and a string quartet. Listen for the moment the string quartet comes in.

genres.name: Varispeed: a piano as harpsichord
genres.text: Lennon wanted a baroque solo in In My Life. George Martin could not play it fast enough, so on 22 October 1965 he recorded his piano solo with the tape at half speed. At normal speed the piano sounded an octave higher, faster and like a harpsichord. With varispeed, changing the tape speed, the Beatles later also altered the sound of voices and whole songs, such as Rain.
genres.listen: Listen to the solo in the middle of In My Life. It is an ordinary piano, but because the tape speed was doubled it sounds like a harpsichord.

genres.name: Day Tripper / We Can Work It Out
genres.text: On 3 December 1965, the same day as Rubber Soul, a single came out with two A-sides: the band could not choose. Day Tripper revolves around a guitar riff by Lennon, a nod to people who only half take part in drug culture. We Can Work It Out has a cheerful verse by McCartney and a gloomy middle section by Lennon in waltz time, with a harmonium.
genres.listen: Compare both sides: in Day Tripper everything revolves around the riff, in We Can Work It Out around the contrast between verse and middle section.

genres.name: Rubber Soul
genres.text: Rubber Soul, released on 3 December 1965, was made in a little over a month, but it feels like an album and not a collection of singles. The lyrics are more personal and more ambiguous, and you hear a sitar, a fuzz bass and a harpsichord-like piano. On the cover the photo is distorted, stretched as in a funhouse mirror. Brian Wilson of The Beach Boys heard it and wanted to make something better.
genres.listen: Harrison plays sitar in Norwegian Wood, McCartney a fuzz bass in Think for Yourself. In each song, look for the instrument you do not expect.

genres.name: 'More popular than Jesus'
genres.text: On 4 March 1966 the London Evening Standard published an interview by Maureen Cleave with John Lennon. He said that Christianity would disappear and that the Beatles were now more popular than Jesus. In England nobody minded. When the American magazine Datebook repeated the quote in late July, Beatles records were burned in the American South. The 1966 tour became tense and unpleasant as a result.

genres.name: Tape loops: Tomorrow Never Knows
genres.text: On 6 April 1966 the recording of Revolver began, with the twenty-year-old Geoff Emerick as new engineer. The first song was Tomorrow Never Knows, on one chord. At home McCartney made tape loops of sped-up guitars and voices. In the studio those loops ran at the same time on different tape recorders and were mixed in and out live. Lennon wanted to sound like a thousand chanting monks; his voice went through a rotating Leslie speaker.
genres.listen: Listen to the screeching sounds that surface and fade away: those are tape loops. In the second part Lennon's voice sounds as if he comes from far away, through the Leslie speaker.

genres.name: ADT: double vocals at the push of a button
genres.text: Lennon hated doubling his vocals: singing everything twice, exactly the same. Engineer Ken Townsend came up with a solution in the spring of 1966. He played a recording back through a second tape recorder with a small delay, so that it sounded like two voices. It was called Artificial Double Tracking, ADT. It can often be heard on Revolver, and every studio afterwards used something similar.
genres.listen: Listen to the vocals in Eleanor Rigby and Doctor Robert. Does the voice sound single, or is there a second layer just behind it?

genres.name: Backwards
genres.text: On 16 April 1966 the band finished Rain, the B-side of Paperback Writer. At the end Lennon sings a piece of lyric backwards: the tape was played in reverse. Lennon said he discovered it by accident when he played a tape the wrong way round at home, while George Martin claimed the idea for himself. A few days later Harrison made a guitar solo for I'm Only Sleeping that sounds backwards.
genres.listen: Listen to the end of Rain: the words are unintelligible, because the tape runs backwards. In I'm Only Sleeping the guitar sounds sucking and floating.

genres.name: The Beach Boys: Pet Sounds
genres.text: Brian Wilson of The Beach Boys heard Rubber Soul and wanted to make an album on which every song was equally strong. With studio musicians in Los Angeles he made Pet Sounds, with bicycle bells, harpsichord, horns and stacks of voices. The album came out on 16 May 1966. Paul McCartney called God Only Knows one of the most beautiful songs ever written. Without Pet Sounds no Sgt. Pepper, he said later.
genres.listen: In God Only Knows, listen to the instruments you do not expect in a pop band: French horn, harpsichord and sleigh bells. Wilson treats the studio like an orchestra.

genres.name: Paperback Writer / Rain
genres.text: Paperback Writer came out in England on 10 June 1966, with Rain as the B-side. Engineer Geoff Emerick made the bass louder than EMI had allowed until then, by using a loudspeaker as a microphone. The lyric is a letter from a writer to a publisher. For promotion the band made films that were sent to television programmes, so they did not have to come themselves: early music videos.
genres.listen: Listen to McCartney's bass: it is much fuller and louder than on earlier Beatles records.

genres.name: Ravi Shankar and the sitar
genres.text: In 1965, on the set of Help!, George Harrison saw Indian musicians and afterwards bought a sitar, which he played in Norwegian Wood. In June 1966 he met the sitar player Ravi Shankar at a dinner in London. Shankar became his teacher, and in September Harrison travelled to India to take lessons. After that he wrote songs in an Indian style, such as Love You To and Within You Without You.
genres.listen: Listen to how in a raga the melody slowly builds over a drone that keeps sounding, without chord changes as in a pop song.

genres.name: Revolver
genres.text: Revolver came out on 5 August 1966, a few weeks before the last concert. Almost no song could be played live. There is a string octet in Eleanor Rigby, Indian music in Love You To, soul horns in Got to Get You into My Life and tape loops in Tomorrow Never Knows. With engineer Geoff Emerick and EMI's tricks, the studio became an instrument.
genres.listen: Taxman begins with a count-in and coughing, as if it were a demo. Then listen to Here, There and Everywhere: two completely different worlds on one record.

tracks.title: Got to Get You into My Life

genres.name: Last concert: Candlestick Park
genres.text: On 29 August 1966 the Beatles played their last paid concert at Candlestick Park in San Francisco. The stadium was not even sold out. After the death threats over the Jesus quote, the trouble in Manila and the screaming that drowned out everything, nobody felt like it any more. McCartney had a press officer make a cassette recording. The last song was Long Tall Sally. From now on the studio was their stage.
genres.listen: Long Tall Sally by Little Richard was their closer. Listen to the studio version from 1964 and compare McCartney's shriek with Little Richard's.

genres.name: Lennon meets Yoko Ono
genres.text: At the Indica Gallery in London in November 1966, John Lennon saw an exhibition by the Japanese artist Yoko Ono, who belonged to the Fluxus movement. He climbed a small ladder and read the word 'yes' on the ceiling through a magnifying glass. According to Lennon it was 9 November, according to the gallery a few days earlier. Ono introduced him to conceptual art and the avant-garde, and later became his wife.

genres.name: The Mellotron
genres.text: A Mellotron is a keyboard instrument with under every key a piece of tape with a recorded instrument, for example a flute. Lennon had one at home. For Strawberry Fields Forever, McCartney played the famous intro on the Mellotron's flute sound in late November 1966. That brought a new tone colour into pop: not real flutes, but not an electronic sound either.
genres.listen: The first bars of Strawberry Fields Forever are a Mellotron with a flute sound. In Flying you hear the same instrument with other sounds.

genres.name: An orchestra in A Day in the Life
genres.text: On 10 February 1967 an orchestra of forty musicians in evening dress came to Studio One, with red noses and party hats. They were given a strange instruction: to glide from their lowest to their highest note over 24 bars, each at their own tempo. That crescendo was used twice in the song. It ends with a piano chord of E that was struck on several pianos at once and rings out for over forty seconds.
genres.listen: Listen to the two times the orchestra builds from low to high, and then count how long the final chord keeps ringing.

genres.name: Strawberry Fields Forever / Penny Lane
genres.text: Two songs about places from childhood in Liverpool, released as a double A-side in February 1967. Strawberry Fields Forever by Lennon is about the garden of a children's home, Penny Lane by McCartney about a shopping street. The final version of Strawberry Fields is stuck together from two recordings in a different key and at a different tempo; by changing the speed they fitted exactly.
genres.listen: About a minute into Strawberry Fields Forever one recording passes into the other. Can you hear where? In Penny Lane a piccolo trumpet plays the solo, inspired by Bach.

genres.name: Sgt. Pepper's Lonely Hearts Club Band
genres.text: After giving up touring, the Beatles worked for months on one record. McCartney came up with a fictional band, so that they could pretend to be someone else. The album came out on 26 May 1967, with a cover by Peter Blake full of celebrities and, for the first time on a rock album, the lyrics on the back. The songs run into each other. Sgt. Pepper became the symbol of the Summer of Love.
genres.listen: Listen to the transition from the title song to With a Little Help from My Friends, and to the sitars in Within You Without You.

tracks.title: Sgt. Pepper's Lonely Hearts Club Band
Lucy in the Sky with Diamonds

genres.name: Our World: All You Need Is Love
genres.text: On 25 June 1967 Our World was the first live television broadcast by satellite to the whole world. Each country supplied a contribution; England chose the Beatles. Lennon wrote a song with a message that everyone would understand. In Studio One they played All You Need Is Love live with an orchestra, surrounded by friends such as Mick Jagger. An estimated 400 million people watched.
genres.listen: The song begins with the Marseillaise and ends with fragments of Greensleeves, Bach and She Loves You. How many quotations do you recognise?

genres.name: The death of Brian Epstein
genres.text: On 27 August 1967 Brian Epstein was found dead in his house in London, from an overdose of sleeping pills. He was 32. The Beatles were in Bangor in Wales at the time, at a meditation course by the Maharishi Mahesh Yogi. Epstein had always taken care of the business side. Without him the band began to manage itself, with Magical Mystery Tour and Apple as first, mixed results.

genres.name: Magical Mystery Tour
genres.text: In England the songs from the television film came out in December 1967 as a double EP. In America Capitol made an album of it on 27 November, supplemented with the singles of that year. That is why Strawberry Fields Forever, Penny Lane and All You Need Is Love are on it. Later this American version also became the standard in England, and it belongs to the official catalogue.
genres.listen: I Am the Walrus is a collage of an orchestra, a choir and a radio broadcast of King Lear, which was mixed in live during the mixing.

genres.name: Magical Mystery Tour (film)
genres.text: McCartney came up with a television film about a bus trip with actors, friends and strange adventures, without a real script. The film was made in Cornwall and at an airfield in West Malling in Kent, and the BBC broadcast it on 26 December 1967. In black and white, although it had been shot in colour. The criticism was harsh. Even so, there are scenes in it that work as early music videos.
genres.listen: In Harrison's Blue Jay Way you hear organ, cello and voices played backwards, as if it sounds on a foggy night.

genres.name: Rishikesh
genres.text: In mid-February 1968 the Beatles travelled to the Maharishi's ashram in Rishikesh, on the Ganges, for a meditation course. Ringo stayed ten days, McCartney a month, Lennon and Harrison longer. Without television or a studio they wrote dozens of songs on acoustic guitar. Donovan taught Lennon a fingerpicking technique there. A large part of the White Album originated here.
genres.listen: In Dear Prudence you hear the fingerpicking pattern that Lennon learned in Rishikesh. The song is about Prudence Farrow, who stayed in her hut meditating all day.

genres.name: Apple Corps
genres.text: After Epstein's death the Beatles founded their own company: Apple, with a record label, a film division and an electronics workshop. On 14 May 1968 Lennon and McCartney presented it in New York. McCartney called it a kind of Western communism. Hey Jude became the first Apple single and Mary Hopkin the first discovery. Business-wise it became a chaos that divided the band.
genres.listen: Those Were the Days by Mary Hopkin, produced by McCartney, was one of the first Apple hits.

genres.name: Revolution 9
genres.text: Revolution 9 is a sound collage of over eight minutes, the most experimental piece the Beatles ever released. Lennon and Yoko Ono built it in late May and in June 1968 from tape loops, classical fragments, reversed sounds and spoken texts. On 20 June they mixed it live, with tape recorders in three studios at once. It simply sits on the White Album, between pop songs.
genres.listen: Try to count how many times you hear the voice say 'number nine'. It comes from an old exam tape of the Royal Academy of Music.

genres.name: Yellow Submarine (animated film)
genres.text: The animated film Yellow Submarine premiered on 17 July 1968 in London. Art director Heinz Edelmann gave it a colourful pop art style. The Beatles themselves did little: their voices were provided by actors and they appear only briefly at the end. Even so, the film was a success, and its imagery still shapes how many people picture the psychedelic sixties.
genres.listen: In Yellow Submarine you hear sound effects of bells, waves and commands, made with items from the sound cupboard at Abbey Road.

genres.name: Eight-track at Trident
genres.text: EMI was cautious with new equipment, and the eight-track machine at Abbey Road was still in the testing phase. The independent Trident Studios in Soho already had one. On 31 July 1968 the band recorded Hey Jude there, the first Beatles song on eight tracks. Later in 1968 they also worked at Trident, including on Martha My Dear. More tracks meant more room for orchestra and overdubs.
genres.listen: In Martha My Dear, recorded at Trident, you hear McCartney's piano, brass and strings, each with its own place in the mix.

genres.name: Hey Jude
genres.text: McCartney wrote Hey Jude to comfort Julian, Lennon's little son, after his parents' divorce. It became the first single on their own label Apple, released in America on 26 August 1968. The song lasts over seven minutes, four of which are a repeated 'na na na' with an orchestra of 36 musicians. Radio stations played it anyway, and it became their biggest hit in America.
genres.listen: Hear how the song begins with just piano and voice, and how the ending gets fuller and fuller until a whole orchestra sings along.

genres.name: The Beatles (the White Album)
genres.text: The double album The Beatles came out on 22 November 1968, in an entirely white sleeve with only the name embossed. It contains thirty songs in all styles: folk, hard rock, music hall, blues and a sound collage. The members often worked separately, in different studios. In August Ringo even quit for a few weeks. Eric Clapton played the solo in While My Guitar Gently Weeps.
genres.listen: Compare three extremes: Blackbird with just guitar and foot tapping, Helter Skelter as loud as it could be, and Eric Clapton's solo in While My Guitar Gently Weeps.

genres.name: The Get Back sessions
genres.text: On 2 January 1969 the Beatles began rehearsing in a chilly film studio in Twickenham for a TV concert, filmed by Michael Lindsay-Hogg. The idea was back to basics: playing new songs live, without tricks. There was tension, and Harrison walked out on 10 January. In mid-January they moved to their own studio under the Apple office. Billy Preston joined them there.
genres.listen: Don't Let Me Down, the B-side of Get Back, comes from these sessions. Do you hear Billy Preston's electric piano?

genres.name: Yellow Submarine
genres.text: The soundtrack album of the animated film came out in January 1969. It has only four new Beatles songs, including Hey Bulldog and Harrison's It's All Too Much, plus two songs released earlier. The whole second side consists of the orchestral music George Martin wrote for the film. It is the least important Beatles album, but Hey Bulldog shows a hard, swinging band.
genres.listen: Hey Bulldog is built on a piano riff that is doubled by guitar and bass. At the end Lennon and McCartney bark at each other.

genres.name: The rooftop concert
genres.text: On 30 January 1969 the Beatles played with keyboard player Billy Preston on the roof of the Apple office on Savile Row in London. It was their first performance in over two years, and their last. For about 42 minutes the neighbourhood heard new songs, until the police came. The concert was filmed for Let It Be, and a few recordings went straight onto the album.
genres.listen: Dig a Pony and I've Got a Feeling on Let It Be were recorded straight from the roof. Do you hear the cold wind and the looseness of a live performance?

genres.name: Bed-in in Amsterdam
genres.text: Lennon and Ono married on 20 March 1969 in Gibraltar. Five days later they began a bed-in for peace in room 902 of the Hilton in Amsterdam: for a week they received journalists in pyjamas. They used the interest in their marriage as advertising for peace. Lennon wrote a song about it, which he recorded with only McCartney as a Beatles single.
genres.listen: The Ballad of John and Yoko retells the journey like a newspaper report. Lennon and McCartney played all the instruments, just the two of them.

tracks.title: The Ballad of John and Yoko

genres.name: Get Back
genres.text: Get Back arose during the film sessions of January 1969 as a jam. The intention was for the band to go back to its roots: no overdubs, just playing together. Billy Preston played electric piano and even got a credit on the single: 'The Beatles with Billy Preston'. Get Back came out on 11 April 1969 and reached number 1 in England and America.
genres.listen: Listen to Billy Preston's electric piano, which plays the solo. It is a bare band recording without strings or effects.

genres.name: The Moog synthesizer
genres.text: In late 1968 George Harrison bought a Moog in America, a modular synthesizer full of cables and knobs. In August 1969 it stood at Abbey Road. On 5 August Harrison played it for the first time on a Beatles recording, in Because. After that the band also used it in Here Comes the Sun, Maxwell's Silver Hammer and I Want You. Electronic sound was now an ordinary instrument in a pop band.
genres.listen: In Here Comes the Sun the Moog plays along with the guitar and floats above the strings. Does it sound like an instrument you know?

genres.name: Abbey Road
genres.text: After the messy film sessions the Beatles wanted to make one more record like in the old days, with George Martin. Abbey Road came out on 26 September 1969. The cover photo on the zebra crossing was taken on 8 August. Side two is a medley of short songs that run into each other. Harrison wrote two of the best-known songs, Something and Here Comes the Sun.
genres.listen: Listen to the medley on side two from Golden Slumbers: small songs are strung together into one big finale, The End.

genres.name: Let It Be
genres.text: McCartney wrote Let It Be after a dream about his mother Mary, who died when he was fourteen. The song was recorded in January 1969 during the film sessions and came out on 6 March 1970 as a single, a month before the news of the break-up. It is a piano ballad that sounds like a gospel hymn. Two different versions of the guitar solo exist, on the single and on the album.
genres.listen: Listen to the gospel character: piano, organ, a small choir and words that sound like a prayer.

genres.name: The break-up
genres.text: Lennon had told the others in September 1969 that he was leaving, but that stayed secret. On 10 April 1970 the papers reported that McCartney was leaving the band. It came from an interview that was included with the press copies of his solo album. Quarrels over money, management and Allen Klein played a part. In late 1970 McCartney went to court to dissolve the partnership.

genres.name: McCartney
genres.text: Paul McCartney recorded his first solo album largely at home, on a four-track recorder, and played almost all the instruments himself. It came out on 17 April 1970, a week after the news of the break-up. Linda McCartney sings along and took the photographs. It sounds homely and unfinished, but Maybe I'm Amazed became one of his best-known songs. Later he founded the band Wings.
genres.listen: Maybe I'm Amazed lets you hear McCartney as singer, pianist, guitarist and bass player all at once. How does he sound without the other three?

genres.name: Let It Be
genres.text: The recordings of January 1969 lay on the shelf for a year. Lennon and Harrison gave them to the American producer Phil Spector, who added strings and choirs. The album came out on 8 May 1970, after the news of the break-up, but it had been recorded earlier than Abbey Road. McCartney was furious about the arrangements of The Long and Winding Road.
genres.listen: Listen to The Long and Winding Road with Spector's strings and choir. Compare it with the bare Two of Us, which has stayed almost as the band played it.

genres.name: Let It Be (film)
genres.text: The film about the sessions of January 1969 premiered on 13 May 1970 in New York, a month after the news of the break-up. None of the Beatles came to watch. The audience saw a band that quarrelled and seemed bored, and the rooftop concert as the ending. As a result Let It Be was long seen as the film about the end. Only much later was it viewed in a more nuanced way.
genres.listen: One After 909 is one of the first songs Lennon and McCartney wrote in the late fifties. On the roof they played it one more time, ten years later.

genres.name: All Things Must Pass
genres.text: George Harrison had been given little room for his songs in the Beatles. After the break-up he released a triple album on 27 November 1970, made with producer Phil Spector and musicians such as Eric Clapton and Ringo Starr. My Sweet Lord became a worldwide hit, although a judge later ruled that it unconsciously resembled He's So Fine by The Chiffons.
genres.listen: In My Sweet Lord the 'hallelujah' in the chorus slowly turns into Hindu prayers. Listen for Harrison's slide guitar, his signature as a soloist.

genres.name: The Concert for Bangladesh
genres.text: Ravi Shankar asked Harrison for help for refugees from Bangladesh, hit by war and floods. On 1 August 1971 they organised two concerts at Madison Square Garden, with Shankar, Bob Dylan, Eric Clapton, Ringo Starr and Billy Preston. It was the first big charity concert in pop, and an example for later events such as Live Aid.
genres.listen: In Bangla Desh, the single Harrison wrote for the concert, he explains in the first lines why he took action.

genres.name: Imagine
genres.text: John Lennon recorded Imagine largely in the studio in his house, Tittenhurst Park near Ascot, with Phil Spector as co-producer. The album came out in September 1971 in America. The title song, sung at a white grand piano, asks the listener to imagine a world without countries, religion and possessions. Lennon said later that the idea came in large part from Yoko Ono.
genres.listen: Imagine is simple: piano, a soft string arrangement and a voice. Why does such a bare arrangement work for such a big message?

genres.name: Ringo
genres.text: On Ringo, released in November 1973, all four former Beatles played, although they were never in the studio all four at the same time. Lennon, McCartney and Harrison each wrote a song for Ringo. Photograph, which he wrote together with Harrison, became a number 1 hit in America. The album showed that the friendship was not entirely broken, and fed rumours of a reunion for years.
genres.listen: Photograph was written by Starr and Harrison. Do you hear the Spector-like wall of sound with choirs and saxophone?

genres.name: Wings: Band on the Run
genres.text: In late 1973 Band on the Run by Paul McCartney and his band Wings came out. Just before the recording the guitarist and the drummer quit. With Linda McCartney and Denny Laine, Paul recorded the album anyway, in an EMI studio in Lagos, Nigeria. There they were robbed of a bag with lyrics and demos. The album reached number one in England and America and is considered his best work after the Beatles.
genres.listen: The title song consists of three different parts in a row. Hear how it goes from slow and gloomy to a cheerful escape.

genres.name: The murder of John Lennon
genres.text: After five years as a househusband, Lennon released the album Double Fantasy with Yoko Ono in November 1980. On 8 December 1980 he was shot dead at the entrance of the Dakota building in New York by a man who had earlier that day got an autograph from him. Lennon was forty. People gathered all over the world, and a reunion of the Beatles was impossible for good.
genres.listen: (Just Like) Starting Over was the first single from Double Fantasy. In his singing Lennon winks at the rock 'n' roll of Elvis and Roy Orbison from his youth.

genres.name: The Beatles Anthology
genres.text: With Anthology the Beatles told their own history: a documentary series, broadcast from 19 November 1995, three double CDs with demos and alternative recordings, and a book. McCartney, Harrison and Starr, with producer Jeff Lynne, made new Beatles songs from two home demos by Lennon: Free as a Bird and Real Love. Anthology 1 also contained the Quarrymen recording from 1958.
genres.listen: Free as a Bird is built on a cassette demo by Lennon from the seventies. Can you hear that his voice sounds thinner than the others'?

genres.name: Now and Then
genres.text: Now and Then was a third Lennon demo that had been left in 1995, because his voice could not be separated well from the piano. For the documentary Get Back, Peter Jackson's team developed software that can separate voices and instruments from a recording. With it McCartney and Starr finished the song, with a guitar part by Harrison from 1995. It came out on 2 November 2023 as the last Beatles single.
genres.listen: Listen to how clear Lennon's voice sounds now, compared with Free as a Bird. The difference comes from the software that separated the voice from the piano.

genres.name: Stuart Sutcliffe
genres.text: In 1960 Stuart Sutcliffe, a friend of Lennon's from art college, became the band's bass player. He was above all a talented painter: one of his canvases was bought by the wealthy art collector John Moores. With Lennon he came up with the name Beetles, after Buddy Holly's Crickets. In Hamburg he fell in love with the photographer Astrid Kirchherr. In 1961 he quit to paint, and in April 1962 he died in Hamburg.
genres.listen: Cayenne is an instrumental by McCartney, recorded at home in 1960. Sutcliffe plays the bass, an instrument he had only just learned to play.

genres.name: The death of George Harrison
genres.text: George Harrison died on 29 November 2001 in Los Angeles of lung cancer; he was 58. According to Hindu custom his ashes were scattered in India. His son Dhani and Jeff Lynne finished his last album Brainwashed, which came out a year later. Exactly a year after his death Eric Clapton, Paul McCartney, Ringo Starr and Ravi Shankar played the Concert for George at the Royal Albert Hall.
genres.listen: Listen to the guitar in Something: Harrison does not play a solo full of notes, but a melody you can sing along with. Compare it with the slide guitar in Any Road.

genres.name: The death of George Martin
genres.text: George Martin, the producer who gave the Beatles a contract in 1962, died on 8 March 2016 at home in Wiltshire, aged 90. He translated their ideas into strings, brass and studio tricks, and was knighted in 1996. With his son Giles he made LOVE in 2006, a mix of Beatles recordings for a Cirque du Soleil show. Paul McCartney called him 'the fifth Beatle'.
genres.listen: Listen to the solo in In My Life: Martin played it on piano, at half speed, and then ran the tape at double speed. That is why it sounds like a harpsichord. In Eleanor Rigby, hear his arrangement for strings alone.
